passage:
For three weeks after Sarika's complaint, I did what everyone did. I ate lunch at my desk so I wouldn't have to choose where to sit. When she said good morning, I nodded and looked at my screen.
I told myself it wasn't my fight. But every evening I felt sick about it. I had seen the same fudged safety sheets she had. I just hadn't said anything.
Then one Thursday I saw her eating alone in the stairwell. I sat down two steps below with my tiffin, without a word.
After a while she said, 'You don't have to do this, Lavanya.'
'I know,' I said. 'I want to.'
The next week I told HR, in writing, what I had seen on those sheets. That Friday, two others quietly joined us in the stairwell.

qa.q: Where did Lavanya find Sarika eating?
qa.a: Lavanya found Sarika eating alone in the stairwell.

qa.q: Why did Lavanya feel sick every evening?
qa.a: Lavanya felt guilty for shunning Sarika after seeing the same fudged safety sheets and saying nothing.

qa.q: Which small acts of support made a difference?
qa.a: Sitting with Sarika in the stairwell and then giving HR a written account of the sheets backed her up, and soon two others joined them.

qa.q: What might it have meant to Sarika when Lavanya sat down with her?
qa.a: After weeks of being shunned, it likely brought relief and showed her she wasn't completely alone.

grounding: It shows a colleague feeling guilt at shunning a truth-teller and then offering small support, a shared lunch and a written statement, that shifts the atmosphere.

passage:
Personal notes, lab section head, 9 August
Vijay has been in the lab six months. Since his report about the altered test results went to management, the team has closed ranks. Chairs get moved when he sits down. His name was left off the Friday birthday email. Yesterday someone wrote 'snitch' in the dust on his cabinet.
I have stayed out of it. Keeping my head down, I told myself. Writing this, I can see that was just silence with a nicer name, and I am not proud of it.
What I did today: wiped the cabinet clean. Asked Vijay to join me for lunch in the canteen, at the centre table. Told him I would give a statement about the cabinet if he wants one.
He said thank you twice. His hands were shaking a little.
- Sarita

qa.q: What was written in the dust on Vijay's cabinet?
qa.a: Someone wrote 'snitch' in the dust on his cabinet.

qa.q: What does Sarita feel about having stayed out of it?
qa.a: Sarita feels guilty, seeing that keeping a head down was really silence, and is not proud of it.

qa.q: What small acts of support does Sarita choose, and why do they matter?
qa.a: Wiping the cabinet, eating with Vijay at the centre table and offering a statement show the team openly that he isn't alone, which can shift the atmosphere.

qa.q: What does Vijay's thanking twice with shaking hands suggest about his experience?
qa.a: It suggests he has been under great strain and isolation, and a single act of support means a lot to him.

grounding: It shows a senior colleague feeling guilt at watching a truth-teller shunned and then choosing small, visible acts of support.

passage:
Thursday
Eshaan ate lunch alone again today. Since he reported the fake test results to compliance, the whole floor treats him as if he's radioactive. Today someone left a sticky note on his monitor: "Snitch." He peeled it off and put it in his drawer without a word.
And I sat three tables away and said nothing. Again. I agree with him. I saw the same results. I just didn't have the guts.
I feel sick about it. Every day I stay quiet, I'm part of it.
So tonight I decided on three small things I can actually do. One: sit with him at lunch tomorrow, even if people stare. Two: tell him, privately, that I saw the same data and will say so if the investigators ask. Three: message him on Sunday, just to check how he's holding up.
It's not heroic. But it's more than silence.
Sangeeta

qa.q: What did someone leave on Eshaan's monitor?
qa.a: A sticky note: Snitch.

qa.q: What is Sangeeta feeling about staying silent?
qa.a: Sangeeta feels guilty and sick, knowing each day of silence makes her part of the shunning.

qa.q: Why do Sangeeta's three small actions matter?
qa.a: Sitting with him, offering to be a witness and checking in give Eshaan real support and can begin to shift the atmosphere.

qa.q: What might Eshaan be going through as he pockets the note?
qa.a: Eshaan likely feels hurt and isolated, trying to stay composed while being shunned for telling the truth.

grounding: A colleague sees a truth-teller shunned, feels guilt at her silence, and decides on small acts of support: company, a witness offer and a check-in.

passage:
At the cooperative bank branch in Kolar, everyone knew why Bhavna now sat at the far counter by the leaking window. Two months ago she had written to head office about loans being given to the chairman's relatives without papers. Since then the staff tea circle had quietly closed without her.
Karthik, the clerk at the next counter, had seen the same files. He hadn't written anything. Each evening, watching Bhavna walk to the bus stand alone, he felt a heavy guilt settle on his shoulders.
On Saturday he made himself do one thing. He carried two cups of tea to her counter, set one down and said, loudly enough for the branch to hear, "Madam, your tea."
The room went quiet. Then the old peon, Rangappa, nodded at Bhavna too.
On Monday Karthik wrote a short note to head office confirming the files he had seen, with dates. It was a small thing. But the next week, two others started sitting with Bhavna at tea.

qa.q: Where did Bhavna sit after writing to head office?
qa.a: At the far counter by the leaking window.

qa.q: What did Karthik feel watching Bhavna walk to the bus stand alone?
qa.a: Karthik felt a heavy guilt for staying silent while she was shunned.

qa.q: How did Karthik's small acts shift the atmosphere?
qa.a: Bringing her tea in front of everyone and writing a witness note gave her support, and soon others started sitting with her.

qa.q: What might Bhavna feel when Karthik sets down the tea?
qa.a: Bhavna likely feels surprised and moved, less alone after weeks of being frozen out.

grounding: In a small-town bank, a clerk who stayed silent while a truth-teller was shunned breaks the freeze with tea in public and a witness note.

passage: Layla had been the only one in the Toronto lab to report that the drug trial data had been cleaned up before submission. Since the review, nobody sat with her at lunch. Xin watched it every day from the next bench: Layla eating alone by the window, the team's weekend plans made loudly in front of her, the jokes about "our compliance officer." Xin had seen the same altered spreadsheet. Xin had said nothing, and every lunch felt heavier for it. On Friday, Xin stopped at Layla's bench on the way out and said quietly, "What you did took courage. If the review needs another person who saw the spreadsheet, I'll give a statement." Layla looked up, eyes wet. On Monday, Xin carried two coffees to the window table and sat down. Two other colleagues glanced over. By Wednesday one of them had joined.

qa.q: Where did Layla eat alone every day?
qa.a: Layla ate alone by the window.

qa.q: What was Xin feeling while watching Layla eat alone?
qa.a: Xin felt guilty for staying silent after seeing the same altered spreadsheet, and every lunch felt heavier for it.

qa.q: Which small acts of support made a difference here?
qa.a: Xin's quiet word of respect, the offer of a witness statement and simply sitting with Layla at lunch changed the mood, so another colleague joined.

qa.q: What is it like for Layla when Xin speaks to her on Friday?
qa.a: Layla is moved and relieved, eyes wet, to learn she is not completely alone after weeks of being shunned.

grounding: Shows a colleague who feels guilty at staying silent while a truth-teller is shunned, and small acts of support that shift the atmosphere.
